title: What a Physical Theory Must Say
question: Why can experiments not fix a physical theory, and what kind of starting point can?
prerequisites: None. This chapter fixes the language used in the rest of the course.
example: The same table of Stern–Gerlach outcomes, explained by two incompatible theories.
principle: Framework: a theory must predict the statistics of repeated, identically prepared experiments.
foil: Any finite table of outcomes, which many theories fit equally well.

sections.title: The Plan of the Course
subsections: Foils: theories that break one principle

title: States as Predictions
question: What is a state, if it is defined only by what it predicts?
prerequisites: Chapter 1: preparations, measurements, and relative frequencies.
example: A coin, a die, and a polarizer, each described only by outcome probabilities.
principle: Mixing: any two preparations can be combined by a random choice.
foil: A theory in which mixing is forbidden, so that states need not form a convex set.

sections.title: Fiducial Measurements
subsections: Finitely many numbers fix a state

title: Effects and Measurements
question: What does a measurement outcome do to a state, mathematically, and how many states can be told apart?
prerequisites: Chapter 2: convex state spaces, fiducial measurements, and linearity.
example: Four state spaces with two perfectly distinguishable states: a segment, a square, a disc, and a ball.
principle: Outcome probabilities are linear functions of the state, and the outcomes of a measurement exhaust all possibilities.
foil: The square bit (gbit), whose state space is a square.

sections.title: Effects
subsections: The unit effect and complete measurements

title: Composite Systems
question: How must a theory describe two systems together if it describes each alone?
prerequisites: Chapters 2 and 3: states, effects, the parameters K and N.
example: Two separated laboratories that each measure one of two bits.
principle: No-signaling and local tomography: joint states are fixed by local measurements and their correlations.
foil: Boxworld, whose PR boxes reach the algebraic maximum of the CHSH expression.

sections.title: Causality and No-Signaling
subsections: Local statistics cannot depend on distant choices

title: Classical Theory and Its Limits
question: Classical probability satisfies every principle so far. What can it not do?
prerequisites: Chapters 2–4: states, effects, distinguishability, and composition.
example: A classical bit that must change from 0 to 1 within one second.
principle: The question: can every pure state be reached from every other by a continuous reversible change?
foil: Classical probability theory itself, whose reversible transformations are permutations.

sections.title: Reversibility in Classical Theory
subsections: No continuous path between pure states

sections.title: Counting Parameters
subsections: The relation between K and N
Hardy’s choice: K = N or K = N²

title: Continuous Reversibility
question: What follows if every pure state can be turned into any other continuously and reversibly?
prerequisites: Chapter 5: the classical simplex and why its reversible maps are discrete.
example: A system that changes smoothly from one of two perfectly distinguishable states to the other.
principle: Continuous reversibility: the reversible transformations form a connected group acting transitively on pure states.
foil: Classical theory, which has distinguishable pure states but no continuous reversible path between them.

title: The Qubit
question: Which ball is the state space of the simplest system, and why does it need complex numbers?
prerequisites: Chapter 6: the state space of a two-outcome system is a ball of some dimension.
example: Two qubits that interact reversibly and continuously.
principle: Local tomography together with continuous reversible interaction between two bits.
foil: Real quantum theory (the disc) and quaternionic quantum theory (the five-dimensional ball).

sections.title: The Probability Rule
subsections: The Born rule for a qubit

title: Larger Systems
question: How do qubits determine the description of every finite system?
prerequisites: Chapter 7: the qubit, its density matrices, and the probability rule.
example: A spin-1 particle with three perfectly distinguishable states.
principle: Equivalence of subspaces, and the availability of all measurements consistent with the state space.
foil: Theories with restricted measurements, and Hardy’s classical branch K = N.

sections.title: Equivalence of Subspaces
subsections: Every two-outcome face is a qubit

sections.title: Hilbert Space
subsections: Density operators and pure states as rays

title: Symmetry and Dynamics
question: What form must reversible change take, and where does the Schrödinger equation come from?
prerequisites: Chapter 8: density operators, pure states, and transition probabilities.
example: A spin in a uniform magnetic field.
principle: Reversible transformations preserve transition probabilities and depend continuously on time.
foil: Antiunitary evolution, which preserves probabilities but cannot be reached continuously from doing nothing.

title: Observables and Uncertainty
question: Why are physical quantities represented by self-adjoint operators?
prerequisites: Chapters 8 and 9: projective measurements and Hamiltonians as generators.
principle: An observable is a measurement whose outcomes are labelled by real numbers.
foil: Hidden-value models in which every quantity has a value before it is measured.

title: Measurement and State Update
question: How does a state change when a measurement reveals an outcome?
prerequisites: Chapter 10: projective measurements, compatibility, and commutation.
example: Three Stern–Gerlach devices in sequence: z, then x, then z.
principle: Repeatable measurements that disturb the state as little as their outcome requires.
foil: Measurement as passive reading of pre-existing values.

sections.title: Instruments
subsections: Probabilities do not fix the update

title: Contextuality and the Born Rule
question: Could measurement outcomes be fixed in advance, and are probabilities other than the Born rule possible?
prerequisites: Chapters 8–11: projective measurements, observables, and compatibility.
example: The Peres–Mermin square of nine two-qubit observables.
principle: Probabilities are assigned to projectors independently of the measurement in which they occur.

sections.title: Gleason’s Theorem
subsections: The Born rule without further assumptions

title: Entanglement and Nonlocality
question: What correlations do quantum composites allow, and why not more?
prerequisites: Chapters 4, 7, and 8: composition, local tomography, and Hilbert space.
example: A Bell pair shared by two distant laboratories.
principle: Local tomography realized as the tensor product of Hilbert spaces.
foil: Local hidden-variable models below, and boxworld above.

sections.title: Reduced States
subsections: Pure joint states with mixed parts

sections.title: Bell Inequalities
subsections: The CHSH bound for local models

title: Indistinguishable Systems
question: What changes when two systems cannot be told apart by any measurement?
prerequisites: Chapters 9 and 13: symmetry and composite systems.
example: Two photons meeting at a beam splitter.
principle: Operational indistinguishability: no measurement can depend on which system carries which label.
foil: Labelled particles, and the parastatistics that the principle alone does not exclude.

sections.title: Indistinguishability
subsections: Labels that no measurement can read

title: Purification and Open Systems
question: How should a system be described when it interacts with an environment we ignore?
prerequisites: Chapters 9, 11, and 13: unitary dynamics, instruments, and reduced states.
example: A qubit coupled to a second qubit that is then discarded.
principle: Purification: every state is the marginal of a pure state, unique up to reversible change of the purifying system.
foil: Classical theory, in which mixed states have no purification.

sections.title: Purification
subsections: Every mixed state has a pure extension
Uniqueness up to a reversible map

sections.title: Decoherence and Measurement
subsections: What the principles do not settle

title: Infinite Dimensions
question: Which parts of the finite-dimensional derivation survive for position and momentum, and what must be added?
prerequisites: Chapters 8–10: Hilbert space, symmetry, and observables.
example: A particle on a line, translated in space and boosted in velocity.
principle: Galilean symmetry represented by continuous unitary groups.
foil: Finite-dimensional theories, which cannot satisfy the canonical commutation relation.

sections.title: Why Finite Dimensions Are Not Enough

title: What Was Assumed
question: Which principles did the work, what would the world be like without each, and what remains open?
example: The gallery of foil theories, reviewed one last time.
principle: All principles of the course, compared.
foil: Every foil met in the course.
